Do Competitive Elections Get People to Vote?

What eight House elections (2010-2024) can tell us

Bobby Innes-Gold

September 2026

As redistricting debates have swept the country, those in favor of reform have argued that competitive districts are essential for a healthy democracy. One facet of this argument is the (seemingly intuitive) idea that having more competitive districts will encourage more people to participate in the democratic process. From a utility perspective, if your vote is more likely to make a difference, then the benefit of voting is higher. However, past research has been mixed on the causality of this relationship. Here, I look at what the data shows about the link between competitiveness and turnout. Using data from eight House election years and Cook PVI scores from each election cycle to measure competitiveness, I find a real but modest relationship. However, much of the apparent effect is explained by who lives in each district.

This is a descriptive look, not a causal analysis. Competitive districts differ from safe ones in ways that also affect turnout, and observational data can’t fully separate how. The charts included here show the patterns, how much of them competition could plausibly account for, and why answering the causal question calls for a different approach.

1. Most of the variation in turnout doesn’t come from district competitiveness

Turnout varies markedly, both from one election to the next and one district to another. To see what helps to explain the variation, I regressed district turnout on three groups of factors and split the explained variation between them, averaging each group’s contribution over every order in which the groups could be added.

The first group, and easily the most explanatory (53%), was a year fixed effects term, classified below as “Which election”. This term accounts for things like whether it’s a presidential vs. midterm year, or just national conditions that were specific to that year. So, over 50% of the variation in district turnout can be explained by national factors impacting all districts. Other explanations are more district-specific.

The second group is “Demographics”, which consists of the percent of adults 25+ with a bachelor’s degree, the median household income, the percentage of homes owned, and the percentage of adults that are 65+ for each congressional district. These demographic variables explain another 23% of the variation in turnout, with the percentage with a bachelor’s degree as the most explanatory on its own.

The third group is district competitiveness, calculated based on each election year’s cook PVI scores. A district’s lean is taken (in either partisan direction) and converted to a 0-1 score where 1 is a perfectly competitive district and scores near 0 are maximally noncompetitive. Competitiveness explains a very small percentage of variation, at about 2%. The additional 22% isn’t explained by any of these three groups.

The four demographic variables included have clear positive relationships with midterm turnout. Here, I looked exclusively at midterm election years, so that high turnout does not just reflect presidential years. I grouped district results from each midterm into 5-point bands based on the percentage of turnout. Higher-turnout districts are on average older, more college-educated, more likely to own their homes, and wealthier.

2. Competitive districts vote more, but who lives there matters

Turnout rises with competitiveness, as the below chart shows, where districts are grouped into 5-point bands by Cook PVI partisan lean, with turnout averaged.

However, there are compositional demographic differences between competitive and noncompetitive districts, which makes competitiveness’s link to turnout look larger than it is.

Across all the years of data, competitive districts (Cook PVI within 5 points of even) had turnout 7.2 points higher than safe districts (more than 15 points from even), comparing districts within the same election year. When comparing only districts with similar income, education, homeownership, and age, that gap shrinks to 3.5 points. About half of the apparent turnout advantage of competitive districts reflects who lives in them.

3. There aren’t many competitive districts left

At this point, there are a relatively small number of districts deemed competitive, at least as defined by the Cook PVI index. In 2024, 62% of districts leaned by more than 10 points towards one party. Thus the benefits that come from competitiveness only reach a small group of voters.

4. The same districts turn out, election after election

Consistently, the same districts with relatively high turnout in one election have high turnout in the next. The 2014 vs. 2018 midterm comparison above exemplifies this (correlation 0.77).

5. Does a Senate race lift House turnout?

A Senate race on the ballot is associated with about 2 to 3 points higher midterm House turnout, similar in size to the competitiveness gap once demographics are accounted for, but much smaller than the jump in presidential years.

What the data can’t tell us

While the data examined here suggests correlations between turnout and forces like year, demographic variables, and to a lesser extent, district competitiveness, observational data is unable to separate competitiveness from who lives in competitive districts, or say whether a turnout boost lasts. If redistricting made a safe district competitive, would turnout rise, and would it stay elevated?

The literature suggests that there are more individual behavioral responses, such as voting habit formation and the social influence of family and friends, that may be driving voter turnout but are not captured in large aggregate data sources. As a result, I am creating an agent-based model microsimulation that can isolate the effect of competitiveness. After making informed assumptions, this will allow me to simulate, in a controlled environment, a situation where a safe district is made competitive while holding everything else, including who lives there, constant. Each simulated voter decides whether to vote based on their own engagement, the people in their social network, how close their race is, and larger external factors. This will allow me to track whether turnout gains persist or compound across future elections through habit and social networks.

Data and methods

  • Turnout: total House votes cast (MIT Election Data and Science Lab, U.S. House returns) divided by the district’s citizen voting-age population (Census ACS), 2010-2024. Uncontested races are excluded.
  • Partisan lean: Cook Partisan Voter Index (PVI) for each cycle.
  • Competitiveness (0-1): probability that a district with a given lean has a race decided by fewer than 20 points, relative to an even district, estimated from 2024 House results (MIT Election Data and Science Lab).
  • Demographics: Census ACS (college share, median household income, homeownership, share over 65).
  • Senate races: whether the district’s state held a U.S. Senate election that year (MIT Election Data and Science Lab, U.S. Senate returns).
  • Uncontested races: races with a single candidate, or a winning margin of 95% or more, are excluded from turnout analyses because House vote totals in those races do not reflect turnout.

References

  • Moskowitz, D. J., & Schneer, B. (2019). Reevaluating competition and turnout in U.S. House elections. Quarterly Journal of Political Science, 14(2), 191-223. https://www.hks.harvard.edu/publications/reevaluating-competition-and-turnout-us-house-elections
